The blade type is a key factor to consider when choosing an electric razor. You’ll typically choose between two main options: rotary blades and foil blades.

If you usually let your stubble grow out or don’t shave every day, a rotary electric razor is your best bet. Its circular motion and flexible head follow the curves of your face, helping it cut through longer or more uneven hair with ease. Rotary razors work especially well for those with normal to tougher skin and medium to coarse beard density, offering a comfortable and efficient shave even after a few days of growth.

A foil works best for shorter facial hair or when you're aiming for a close shave similar to classic razors. It uses oscillating blades hidden beneath a thin, perforated foil that captures and cuts hairs as they emerge through the mesh. While a foil shaver tends to be noisier than rotary models, it offers deeper precision. To get the smoothest results, use it with straight, steady strokes—moving back and forth along the face and neck. This design makes foil razors ideal for those who shave daily or want clean, sharp lines around facial hair.

Corded razors plug directly into a power source, so you don’t have to worry about charging or replacing batteries. As a result, they deliver more consistent power and longer performance. Since they don’t need to conserve energy, they also usually run stronger than cordless models. That mentioned, cordless razors offer added convenience, especially for travel or grooming on the go, with options powered by either rechargeable or disposable batteries. Ultimately, the right choice depends on your routine and how much flexibility you need.

Many premium models offer additional features or accessories to enhance the shave experience or make it more convenient, including:.

The Men’s Health grooming team has been extensively testing electric razors since 2018. For years, we’ve been putting shavers to the test, evaluating their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use over long periods of time. As someone who can get a five o'clock shadow before lunch, I am constantly shaving. This has given me a consistent canvas to test and retest editor favorites, as well as the latest innovations and newly introduced grooming releases.

For this story, I considered the team’s reviews and notes of top-performing razors dating back eight years, in addition to my own experience, to land on 15 options to extensively test or retest over an 18-month trial period. I’ve also included before-and-after shots of yours truly for most of the razors to show the kind of shave each one delivers. Based on this first-hand use, I narrowed that list to eight, representing the best electric razors for men to buy in 2026.

It has been revealed that both electric and manual razors use blades to cut hair, but they do it in different ways. Manual razors pull each hair up with the first blade, then slice it closer to the skin with the following blades—kind of like using a knife. Electric razors, on the other hand, work more like scissors. Most use a foil system: hair enters tiny holes in the foil, and internal blades cut it from beneath. Rotary versions use a slightly different mechanism, but the concept is similar.

Industry observers note that manual razors shave closer because the blades touch the skin directly. That closeness comes with a downside: higher chances of razor burn, bumps, or ingrown hairs, especially if you skip proper prep or use a dull blade. Electric razors always have a barrier between the blade and skin, so while they won’t shave quite as close, they’re often gentler and better suited for sensitive skin.

Read More: 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Awards.

In a recent development, using an electric razor is much easier to pick up compared to a traditional or safety razor. Still, don’t just grab yours and start shaving right away. Take the time to learn how to get the closest shave possible before speeding through the process for the best results.

Start your shave with clean skin. Whether you’re using a wet or dry shaver, you should tackle your scruff right after washing your face. For dry shavers, apply a small amount of pre-shave oil or wash your face and then gently pat it dry. These shavers perform best when the stubble is firm and completely dry.

According to recent reports, keep the razor at a 90-degree angle to your skin to avoid cutting hairs unevenly. There’s no need to press hard, as a light grip does the job. Pressing down too much, especially around the jaw or chin, can lead to patchy results and irritation. With a foil shaver, I stick to back-and-forth strokes. If I’m using a rotary, I’ll go with either circular or straight motions, depending on what feels best.

Reading the manual might seem unnecessary (and boring), but brands often include specific tips or techniques tailored to their design. Those little details can make a significant difference, resulting in a noticeably smoother shave. It might not be Hemingway, but taking a few minutes to go through the instructions usually pays off in better results and a more comfortable experience overall.

Sources indicate that as long as I stick to proper maintenance and care, I get a consistently smooth shave from electric razors. If you’re latest to these tools, however, give your skin about two weeks to adjust—it makes a big difference. A little patience and upkeep go a long way.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first things I check in an electric razor is how easy it is to clean because this will help both its effectiveness and longevity (not to mention my blood pressure). Skipping regular cleaning can clog the blades with hair and gunk, which not only affects performance but also shortens the razor’s life. When using a waterproof device, I always rinse mine under running water after each use, then use a small brush to clear out any buildup on the foil.

In a recent development, that foil is key to getting a smooth, even shave, but it’s delicate. If it gets bent or damaged, replace it right away. Letting it go risks rough shaves, irritation, or even breakouts from dragging dirt across your skin. Some higher-end models, like the Braun Series 9, come with automatic cleaning stations. They’re super convenient (even if a bit bulky and noisy) and use replaceable cartridges that last around three months—about $5 each in a multi-pack. While not essential, they definitely make it easier to stay on top of maintenance.

Read More: How To Maintain Your Beard Trimmer.

High-quality electric razors—especially those in the $200-plus range—can last years, sometimes even five or more if well maintained. To keep mine running strong, I make sure to replace the blades and foil regularly. Depending on the brand, blade replacement is usually recommended every 6 to 18 months. I also keep an eye on the foil. If it gets dented or damaged, I swap it out immediately since most replacement cartridges include both parts.

Sources indicate that these typically cost between $20 and $50. Battery life is typically the first thing to go. Over time, even the best razors start to lose their charge faster or run with less power. When I notice my shave isn’t as close, or the razor starts pulling instead of cutting cleanly, that’s my cue that it might be time for a upcoming one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It indicates that when the Riemann zeta function equals zero, the solutions other than a known set of exceptions all lie on the same vertical line, where the real part is one-half.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that independent checkers validated Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the Lean and Mathlib communities said on Nov. 21. Teams rebuilt his roughly 17-million-line library, matched its conclusion to the original conjecture and checked each step of the exported proof. They established what the code proved while a complete mathematical write-up was still to come.

The conjecture dates to 1859. It indicates that when the Riemann zeta function equals zero, the solutions other than a known set of exceptions all lie on the same vertical line, where the real part is one-half. Where those zeros lie helps explain how the distribution of prime numbers deviates from its average pattern.

According to recent reports, alpöge released the proof on Nov. 20 as code for Lean, a system for writing and checking mathematical proofs. In his release note, he stated he chose a setting where two mathematical ideas could be combined and credited Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude with suggesting advances late in the argument.

In his MIT-hosted verification logs, Andrew Sutherland reported that a rebuild on a separate machine, with networking disabled and the source files set to read-only, produced a byte-for-byte match to the published proof export. The export contains the formal proof steps in a form that other checkers can read.

In a recent development, in their joint statement, the Lean and Mathlib communities noted they put the target theorem in a separate challenge file that imported only Mathlib, Lean’s library of formalized mathematics. Two comparison tools confirmed that the conclusion in Alpöge’s proof matched Mathlib’s existing statement of the conjecture.

In a recent development, two independently written checkers, nanoda and con-leche, accepted the full export, Sutherland reported. They checked whether the steps justified the conclusion using the exported data, which kept executable code in the original source files out of that part of the process.

Industry observers note that A clean rebuild matched the published export. Verifiers compared the result with Mathlib’s theorem statement and independently checked the proof steps.

Industry observers note that the statement comparison identifies the theorem. The proof checks establish whether the steps justify it.

The diagram covers completed checks for the original conjecture. Clay’s decision follows its own publication and acceptance rules.

The left branch compares the submission with a separately prepared Mathlib challenge. The right branch checks the submitted proof export with two independent implementations.

Sources indicate that the diagram covers completed checks for the original conjecture. Clay’s decision follows its own publication and acceptance rules.

Sutherland’s team also replayed all 175,187 compiled modules through Lean’s own checker. The team’s additional Lean runs on the raw export were still underway in his Nov. 22 upgrade. The checks also covered a generalized version of the conjecture for Dirichlet L-functions.

Industry observers note that alpöge said he planned to write up the proof for mathematicians to read. Michael Rubinstein at the University of Waterloo posted a working guide dated Nov. 21 that explains parts of the argument for the original conjecture. The guide still relies on the Lean development for the proof of a central inequality.

Clay Mathematics Institute’s problem page still listed the conjecture as unsolved when checked on Nov. 22. Under Clay’s prize rules, the institute considers a proposed solution only after publication in a qualifying outlet, at least two years since that publication and general acceptance in the global mathematics community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A year ago, Zcash [ZEC] began a remarkable rally. After gently ticking upward from $34 to $60 in August and September 2025, the privacy token led an explosive sector-wide bullish charge.

On the 1st of October 2025, entrepreneur and angel investor Naval Ravikant posted on X that,.

Sources indicate that bitcoin is insurance against fiat. Zcash is insurance against Bitcoin.

Recent findings suggest that it helped kick off a wave of bullish enthusiasm for ZEC as well as the privacy sector. Zcash surged by 1,135% in five weeks, Dash [DASH] rallied 605%, and Monero [XMR] was up by 181% from early October, though its move took longer, until January 2026.

Neither of the latter two tokens has managed to regain the highs they made back then.

Meanwhile, ZEC reached $1,700. The altcoin’s correction in recent months back below $1,000 has sparked bearish short-term sentiment, even though it was still trading above the previous year’s peak.

According to recent reports, apart from expansion on the price front, the privacy sector leaders have made substantial progress in 2026. The need for privacy is nuanced. Users want confidential smart contracts, not just standalone privacy.

Industry observers note that presently, Monero uses RingCT to hide transactions. RingCT, along with CLSAG ring signatures, enforces a fixed ring size of 16- 15 decoys plus one real input. This makes it harder to trace the address for each transaction, without requiring other customers to break deterministic trails, which privacy methods such as CoinJoin for Bitcoin require.

Sophisticated on-chain analysis can still narrow down to the 16 possibilities over multiple “hops”, or intermediate payments or asset transfers along a transaction trail.

According to recent reports, monero’s Full Chain Membership Proofs++ (FCMP++) eliminates the need for decoys. It replaces rings by providing zero-knowledge membership proofs across the entire blockchain output set. In other words, it mathematically proves that the spent XMR belongs to the Monero blockchain, making every previous output created part of the decoy set.

It has been revealed that A mainnet activation date has not been confirmed for the FCMP++ and Carrot, the addressing protocol and wallet key hierarchy upgrade designed for the FCMP++ network upgrade. AMBCrypto reported that zkSecurity’s audit of FCMP++ was “complete, zero-knowledge, and sound”.

In a recent development, while Monero enforces privacy on every transaction, Zcash gives customers the option of privacy. It has transparent transactions, but also allows the use of zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) when shielded addresses are used.

Industry observers note that using zero-knowledge cryptography, private ZEC balances and transactions are tracked in shielded pools. Zcash has five of these shielded pools, as well as its transparent pool. Once funds are inside, the older pools can not be shut down, but can be made spend-only.

Industry observers note that the Ironwood (NU6.3) upgrade was launched on the 28th of July, 2026, addressing the Orchard “infinity” bug found in May. It also introduced a new shielded pool and restricted the Orchard pool. Funds exiting Orchard must now pass through Zcash’s turnstile, for supply integrity verification, to enter Ironwood.

According to recent reports, the NU7 upgrade implemented in November aims to reduce block processing times by 67%, from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. It also reduced the wallet scanning workload required to perform private payments.

The upgrades are an encouraging sight for long-term users and investors. At the same time, the use case for privacy is also expanding.

Recent findings suggest that when transactions are shielded in some form, anti-money laundering (AML) tracing is hindered or prevented. This brings strict regulatory restrictions on shielded transactions, as they require visibility in fund flows to prevent illicit financing.

As open blockchains, such as Ethereum [ETH] and Solana [SOL], enter the financial mainstream, institutional adoption requires them to address privacy. Their open nature means accessibility risks become a competitive liability and can have legal, financial, or operational repercussions.

Blockchain data and analytics platform Chainalysis wrote that institutional adoption is accelerating privacy network growth. Institutions must choose the right technology for their needs, whether it be shielded pools (like Zcash) or encrypted extensions (like Solana’s confidential transfers).

Canton [CC] is purpose-built for institutions. The network’s sub-transaction privacy hides all transaction details, even the transaction’s existence, from all but the parties involved. This segmented information sharing embeds privacy into the chain.

There is a case to be made for both financial privacy and financial oversight. The former argues for a fundamental right in a world of persistent data collection and financial surveillance.

The latter argues that oversight is a necessity to prevent serious crimes and to detect and disrupt illicit activity.

Elliptic, another blockchain analytics manufacturer that provides crypto compliance software, noted that crypto projects can embed compliance-supporting features without wholly abandoning privacy.

Selective disclosure, such as in Zcash, Midnight, or using Identity Frameworks in Ethereum, can achieve this by sharing transaction details without revealing the entire financial history.

Zero-knowledge compliance is another approach that can prove that a transaction meets certain criteria, without exposing other relevant details.

Finding this middle ground between oversight and privacy is becoming increasingly key to create a secure, yet private, digital future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • According to recent reports, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • Sources indicate that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters stated Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and shows,” according to Bloomberg.

According to recent reports, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Sources indicate that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

Sources indicate that it was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

According to recent reports, there are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

In a recent development, porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters stated customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

Industry observers note that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

According to recent reports, it’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Financial markets, including crypto, need to start preparing now for quantum computers capable of breaking the cryptography that secures them, according to the world's main forum for securities regulators.

A "sufficiently capable" quantum computer could undermine widely used public-key cryptography that supports critical functions across financial markets, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) mentioned in a report published on Thursday. The cyber readiness challenge posed by quantum computing "is immediate and requires action," it said.

"Practical quantum computers capable of compromising widely used cryptography do not yet exist, but the scale and duration of the transition mean the financial sector should start preparing today," IOSCO Board Chair Jean-Paul Servais remarked in a statement.

The 63-page report cited conservative estimates that such machines could emerge between 2030 and 2035. Several industry participants consulted by IOSCO went further, arguing that firms should prepare for the possibility that they arrive within five years, potentially accelerated by AI.

IOSCO said the migration may be particularly challenging for blockchains, because cryptography is embedded in their core architecture and any change requires coordinated action across decentralized networks. Public blockchains such as Ethereum, Solana and Tron rely heavily on elliptic curve cryptography to verify identities and validate transactions, and a powerful enough quantum computer could derive private keys from exposed public keys, a scenario known as "Q-Day.".

In a recent development, swapping in quantum-resistant signatures comes at a cost. Signatures under ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum standard from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, are about 2,420 bytes, roughly 35 to 40 times larger than today's 64-byte elliptic curve signatures, the report mentioned. It cited evidence from a quantum-resistant Solana testnet that saw throughput fall by about 90% when post-quantum signatures replaced existing ones.

Because the cryptography sits in transaction formats and consensus rules, replacing it requires hard forks, and decentralized networks have no way to force quick adoption, making migration "slow and fragmented," IOSCO remarked. Accounts and smart contracts still controlled by vulnerable keys could stay exposed after a network adds quantum-resistant options, and the path to quantum resistance for Bitcoin wallets remains uphill.

Industry observers note that wallet makers face their own trade-offs. SHRINCS, the leading candidate for a post-quantum Bitcoin signature scheme, offers "stateful" signatures that are about 10 times smaller but can expose funds to theft if keys are reused beyond a set signing budget, Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka has stated. Trezor is considering making the larger, safer stateless option the default, and hardware wallets will also need post-quantum cryptography for firmware and device authentication, he added.

Industry observers note that the report distinguished "on-spend" attacks, in which an attacker races to exploit a public key revealed by a pending transaction, from "at-rest" attacks on keys left exposed for longer. Dormant or abandoned coins pose a particular problem where their holders can't move them. Crypto firms have formed a quantum alliance as some 6 million BTC sit in exposed addresses, and Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has proposed "quantum landmines" to make attacks on such coins costly.

Layer-2 networks are not insulated either. Optimistic rollups could face forged signatures during their dispute windows, typically seven days on Ethereum, and many zero-knowledge rollups use SNARK proofs that rely on elliptic curves. Hash-based STARK proofs are more resistant, but a rollup is only as safe as the layer-1 contracts, bridges and governance keys it depends on, the report stated.

Developers are already working on fixes. Researchers have proposed several ways to make Bitcoin quantum-safe, StarkWare has shown a quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction, and Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has said the network is betting its future on quantum resistance.

In a recent development, IOSCO said firms should migrate to post-quantum cryptography and build "crypto-agility," the ability to update cryptographic systems without major redesign. Quantum key distribution could complement those measures on selected high-security channels, it added.

Sources indicate that most preparations across financial markets are still at an early stage, focused on awareness, governance, training and identifying vulnerable systems, according to the report, which drew on a March 2026 survey of members of IOSCO's Fintech Task Force and discussions with experts. Some respondents described "quantum-procrastination," in which firms put off action while waiting for clearer regulatory signals or wider adoption.

Recent findings suggest that no surveyed jurisdiction reported operational deployment of quantum computing in regulated financial services. The watchdog also urged regulators to act against "quantum washing," in which firms overstate the role, maturity or performance of quantum technology. IOSCO said it will treat quantum as a priority in 2027, focusing on raising awareness across the financial ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that quantum hardware is advancing quickly. IBM has claimed a trusted quantum advantage, and Google has stated it has cracked some of the field's biggest bottlenecks.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that crypto exchanges spent the past week rolling out tokenized U.S stocks to buyers around the world.
  • Recent findings suggest that one story is about tokenization, while the other is about AI stocks.
  • According to recent reports, for most people outside the U.S, buying an Apple or Nvidia stock is hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that crypto exchanges spent the past week rolling out tokenized U.S stocks to buyers around the world. On an unrelated note, Nvidia slid by 30% from its ATH in a month following Jensen Huang’s departure. All while AMD rose — an early sign of decoupling.

Recent findings suggest that one story is about tokenization, while the other is about AI stocks. However, both skirt around the same topic: a growing class of investors being handed exposure they don’t fully understand by markets that do not care to explain it.

According to recent reports, for most people outside the U.S, buying an Apple or Nvidia stock is hard. It is either expensive, tedious, or simply unavailable. Pritam Dutta, Founder and CEO of Zoth, explained the same when he spoke to AMBCrypto, stating,.

There’s a lot of excitement around tokenized stocks right now. Most people outside the U.S. still can’t easily buy shares in Apple, Nvidia and the rest of the Magnificent Seven. Tokenization changes that.

Undoubtedly, for a buyer in Nigeria or the Philippines, a tokenized stock could be their first realistic route into U.S markets. But Dutta’s next point is the one that should make an investor sit up and take notice.

A lot of what’s launching gives you price exposure, not the share itself. You don’t get voting rights, and dividends depend on the platform’s terms… Too few platforms are being upfront about it.

In a nutshell, investors are not buying Apple. They are buying a token that tracks Apple’s price, issued by a platform whose terms determine what else you get, subject to its discretion.

Dutta, then, reduced the entire conversation to three questions investors must ask themselves before running towards such stocks.

Who holds the real share? What happens to my dividends? What happens if the platform fails?

These are not clever questions. These are the questions you should ask before buying anything that is marketed as “tokenized.” Unfortunately, the fact that they need to be asked in the first place is a sure-shot sign of how little the platforms are disclosing.

Sources indicate that in today’s age, the access is real, but the understanding might not be. And, that gap is the hardest on buyers with the least room to make an error.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia fell this week while AMD rose. The easy explanation is Jensen Huang’s exit. However, Ian Weisberger, CEO of CoinRoutes, believes that there is a larger cause. He told AMBCrypto,.

The real problem is that Nvidia’s chips are becoming a commodity.

It has been revealed that for years, Nvidia and the AI boom were not seen as two separate entities, simply because of the former’s chips. That is also how the company grew to roughly 8% of the S&P 500.

This week, though the market began pulling the two apart — and within the AI sector — the separation was underway long before anyone realized.

Anyone who has built on both stacks knows the gap is closing. As the chips become interchangeable, buyers will shop on price, and the profits will move to the companies building products on top of them.

That is the concentration problem in one paragraph. When a single stock is 8% of the AI sector, millions of retail investors own a large position in it through their index funds. That is exposure they never signed up to be a part of.

The AI boom is not ending, but the era of one stock carrying the index might be.

According to recent reports, both stories have the same problem — the people most likely to be hurt are unfortunately the least equipped to protect themselves. Here’s why.

It has been revealed that firstly, tokenized stocks are best for an overseas buyer for whom a U.S brokerage account is out of reach. Unfortunately, that buyer is also the first to suffer losses if their platform of choice fails.

Secondly, when it comes to artificial intelligence, the cracks are less noticeable. Most overseas retail investors own Nvidia through an index fund that was marketed to them as “diversified.” This causes the investor with the least information to hold one of the most crucial market bets.

As Nicolai Sondergaard, research analyst at Nansen, told AMBCrypto:.

AI and crypto draw on the same pool of risk capital, so when Nvidia sells off, the money goes to cash, not into Bitcoin.

At the time of Sondergaard’s analysis, Nvidia was down about 32% from its 6th October high, Bitcoin [BTC] was 26% below its September peak, and gold was 17% off its August high. Meanwhile, the dollar was at a six-month high, and real yields were up more than 0.2 percentage points in two months.

Recent findings suggest that so, the investor who thought they were spread across AI and crypto was actually holding double the risk. And in the worst case, they must have not figured it out before it was too late.

The same story can be crafted across different markets — the sophisticated investor can take on the risk, while the overseas investor cannot. Regardless, the product holds no difference when marketing to them.

The demand is real. The question is whether people are being sold what they think they’re buying.

The question at the end of it all is — were buyers sold a dream that was impossible to achieve? Looking further, was the promised portfolio diversification ever there at all?

Recent findings suggest that in the end, the retail investor’s blind spot is not ignorance. It is the industry that keeps expanding faster than investors understand what’s going on, causing them to buy the narrative and allure. Not the reality.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once a Fluid borrower has repaid their USDC loan and reclaimed eligible hBTC collateral, they hold a Bitcoin-backed token on Sui. To get native Bitcoin into their wallet, they need a separate redemption from Hashi, the protocol that issues hBTC. Hashi’s payout limit can hold up an approved withdrawal even when the pool has enough BTC to cover it.

Fluid declared its hBTC lending markets on Nov. 20, a day after the Sui Foundation announced the market was live. Bitcoin holders can deposit BTC with Hashi, receive hBTC on the Sui network and pledge that token to borrow USDC, the first stablecoin available through the market.

The underlying coins remain on Bitcoin at an address derived for the depositor’s Sui account. Hashi’s deposit guide describes who can spend them in the normal withdrawal process. Validators in Hashi’s committee provide one authorization collectively, and a separate signer called the Guardian provides the other. Once the borrower has the hBTC back on Sui, those signers still have to authorize the Bitcoin payout.

In a recent development, once a borrower has the hBTC back, they can request a withdrawal on Sui by submitting the amount and a compatible Bitcoin address. Hashi sets the hBTC aside and queues the request while it waits for a quorum of committee members to approve the request. The committee leader gathers approved requests into a batch so several owners can receive Bitcoin in a single transaction.

Hashi burns the hBTC when the leader commits the batch. The committee jointly produces one signature for each Bitcoin input the batch spends. The Guardian checks the batch against its limit and supplies a second signature for each input. Once the transaction is fully signed, the leader broadcasts it, with each user’s share of the miner fee deducted from their payout. Hashi marks the withdrawal confirmed after the transaction reaches its required number of Bitcoin confirmations.

The Guardian’s withdrawal limit has two settings. One sets the maximum amount the system can release at once. The other determines how rapidly capacity refills after a payout batch uses it. The pool balance measures the Bitcoin held by Hashi, while the limit governs how much of that Bitcoin can move at a given time.

If an approved request is within the maximum but is too large for the capacity available at that moment, it waits for room to open up. Requests behind it can wait too. Hashi skips requests above the maximum until governance raises the limit. The borrower can cancel and recover their hBTC after a cooldown, up until the leader commits the request to a batch.

The result depends on how much capacity the Guardian has available and whether the request fits the configured maximum.

Hashi can hold enough BTC even when the Guardian has too little payout capacity for a particular request.

The live maximum, refill rate and elapsed withdrawal times remain unverified.

Sources indicate that the diagram maps the queue outcomes in Hashi’s documented withdrawal lifecycle and Guardian rate limiter. The three branches illustrate rules and use no numerical scale.

The live maximum, refill rate and elapsed withdrawal times remain unverified.

Hashi describes roughly five minutes from submission as one trigger for building a batch. The full withdrawal also depends on approval, available payout capacity, signatures and Bitcoin confirmations. Hashi’s withdrawal FAQ describes how to check current capacity. The deployed maximum and refill rate remain unverified, as does the time from repayment to a Bitcoin payout for a Fluid borrower.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 21, Merkl’s Fluid lending campaign displayed $862.26K in total value locked in its Sui fUSDC rewards opportunity. The figure captures activity on the lender side of the market. The amount of USDC borrowers have drawn against hBTC remains unverified.

Fluid states Anchorage Digital’s institutional clients can lend USDC or borrow it against hBTC on the protocol. Anchorage Digital Bank N.A. provides custody and settlement services. The Sui Foundation says institutions can already use Anchorage’s self-custody wallet, Porto, to access hBTC and select Fluid strategies. It expects tri-party settlement in early 2027. Anchorage identifies Atlas as its tri-party route for institutions that keep assets in qualified custody.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Industry observers note that starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, remarked (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

Industry observers note that the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a latest vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

It has been revealed that subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante remarked the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Renowned financial guru and Rich Dad Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has offered compelling insight into the reasons behind his buying spree of Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH) despite the current crypto market crash.

Kiyosaki, who is an esteemed investor, predicts that a financial crisis could be on the horizon, and it might be even worse than the 2008 market crash. He believes that crypto assets and other hard assets are an effective hedge against the repercussions of government-induced overborrowing and money printing.

The financial guru's latest X post explains his rationale behind investing in Bitcoin, Ethereum, gold, silver, real estate, and oil instead of traditional financial assets.

"Why I am buying real (no ETFs) gold, silver, Bitcoin, and Ethereum," Kiyosaki noted in his latest post.

He attributed his views to the Federal Reserve, the U.S. Treasury and the colossal debt obligations of the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that according to Kiyosaki, the government's inability to curb spending will lead to massive money printing in the future. This might erode the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar.

"The BIG PRINT is about to begin," Kiyosaki warned.

In a recent development, this is the core reason for his investments in Bitcoin and Ethereum. He believes that these assets will rise in value when the government is forced to aggressively print money in response to escalating financial concerns.

Moreover, he believes that holding these crypto assets directly would be better than investing in exchange-traded funds (ETFs). However, he did not offer a reason for his opposition to ETFs in his post.

Furthermore, Kiyosaki stated that the next financial crisis could be much bigger than the global financial crisis of 2008.

"This crash we are just now sliding into is much bigger than 2008. Possibly a global depression," he commented.

He also mentioned that his gold, silver, Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings could make him one of the ultra-rich if his predictions come true.

Industry observers note that however, Kiyosaki mentioned some figures that were not entirely accurate. For instance, he stated that the U.S. national debt stood at $49 trillion. But according to Treasury data, the national debt was about $40.7 trillion in November 2026. Also, his claim that the U.S. is printing $1 trillion every 90 days conflates government debt with money printing.

Although Kiyosaki is a strong believer in Bitcoin, he recently advised investors not to buy Bitcoin immediately amid the digital asset's current price slump.

On Nov. 20, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author cautioned against catching a 'falling knife.'.

"Never grab a falling knife." This means that investors should wait for the market crash to end before buying.

"I started buying bitcoin around $20k after the market crashed last time," Kiyosaki recalled.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," he added.

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the latest IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the latest IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

It has been revealed that the IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai mentioned the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

In a recent development, it uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

Sources indicate that that’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a upcoming Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

Industry observers note that on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an patch. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

According to recent reports, hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

Sources indicate that with the 2027 models on the way, you may be able to score some deals on Hyundai’s current EV lineup. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

Industry News: Rethinking crypto risk — Here’s why ONE factor doesn’t tell the whole story

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that investors have a habit of gauging crypto by a single risk framework.
  • Bitcoin’s [BTC] daily price fluctuations are about three times wider than the S&P 500’s, with far more extreme moves in both directions.
  • So, investors should be aware of three things — where returns come from, how they fit inside a portfolio, and how crypto has grown far beyond Bitcoin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that investors have a habit of gauging crypto by a single risk framework. However, at the moment, that framework no longer captures how the market works.

Bitcoin’s [BTC] daily price fluctuations are about three times wider than the S&P 500’s, with far more extreme moves in both directions. However, the realized volatility of Bitcoin has declined over time to the level of individual large-cap U.S stocks.

So, investors should be aware of three things — where returns come from, how they fit inside a portfolio, and how crypto has grown far beyond Bitcoin.

In a recent development, the standard risk tools like the standard deviation or the Sharpe ratio don’t care how much money you make or lose. That leaves a blind spot for Bitcoin as most of its long-term gains come from just a handful of trading days.

Industry observers note that bitcoin has averaged 60% per year over the last three years. If you take away its ten best days, that number drops to 7%. If you take away its ten worst days, the number jumps to 197%. That’s because big drops are often followed by big rebounds, so investors who try to avoid bad days can easily miss the best ones.

Momentum counts as well. Bitcoin’s gains tend to pile on top of each other, and Bitcoin runs far better after months of winning than months of losing. During strong rallies, the Sortino ratio can rise well above normal risk scores. Mostly because it only measures returns against downside volatility, not upside volatility.

Notably, Bitcoin has dropped by 50% or more seven times since 2011. But when you include the volatility of starting, Bitcoin’s falls look more like stocks and bonds.

In fact, even “low risk” bonds have been falling for a while in recent years.

While substantial price moves can be alarming on their own, portfolio managers care most about how an asset behaves when put together with the other assets they own. Changes in stocks, bonds, and the private market are mostly driven by common economic factors. However, these factors explain the changes in Bitcoin much less.

Cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, have historically shown low correlation with traditional measures than with each other. This is the case, even though correlations can increase during periods of market stress.

Sources indicate that large organizations have taken this into account too. For instance, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, an organization with $5 trillion in assets, introduced Bitcoin into its 2027 outlook, estimating a 10% per year return in the coming ten years. This correlates by only 33% with major U.S. equities, even less than international equities, corporate bonds, and hedge funds, even when there is 55% volatility.

Industry observers note that this provides a unique combination of both high expected returns and little correlation with core equities. History proves that including a small portion of Bitcoin in an average institutional portfolio can increase returns and efficiency without increasing overall risk or maximum losses.

Recent findings suggest that notably, Mike Belshe, CEO of BitGo, recently pointed out JPMorgan’s changing perspective on crypto. He mentioned,.

Sources indicate that let that sink in. The world’s largest bank, long crypto-skeptical, is now publicly supporting crypto market structure legislation. This is a different ballgame.

Another mistake is treating crypto as a single Bitcoin bet. The modern landscape of crypto includes smart contract platforms, decentralized finance, consumer applications, and artificial intelligence. Each having its own unique users and economics.

Over the last three years, Bitcoin has accounted for just about 50% of volatility in returns on all major crypto sectors, while correlations among sectors have decreased.

Out of the top 10 biggest non-stablecoin crypto assets by market cap, six different tokens have been leading returns on a quarter-by-quarter basis over the last two years. Bitcoin has never led once.

In a recent development, none of this implies that crypto is risk-free though. Especially since a rally could unwind rapidly. On the contrary, risk is not something that can be boiled down to one simple figure.

A uniform know-how about crypto implies understanding of multiple factors — volatility of the asset, distribution of returns, correlation with the rest of a portfolio, and the performance of various sectors separately.

Therefore, in reality, instead of trying to overlook any price fluctuations, it is important to view them with a proper perspective.

Rather than discussing the volatility of crypto per se, one should think of what kind of risks it introduces, what risks from one’s portfolio it offsets, and what additional sources of profit appear outside of Bitcoin.

Industry News: Solana’s new memory checks could make some older app transactions fail

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cryptoslate

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that solana’s planned memory checks could make some app transactions fail even when the rest of the app keeps working.
  • Anza, which develops Solana’s Agave validator software, resumed general mainnet feature activations on November 19.
  • Anza’s November 20 tracker listed both switches as pending on Solana mainnet, with no activation slot for either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that solana’s planned memory checks could make some app transactions fail even when the rest of the app keeps working. Developers have already seen one example in replayed mainnet transactions. Older code built with the Anchor framework could try to save an account’s data after handing control of that account to another program.

Anza, which develops Solana’s Agave validator software, resumed general mainnet feature activations on November 19. Its November 20 feature tracker lists the memory checks and a separate change called account data direct mapping as pending, with no mainnet activation epoch or slot for either. Direct mapping is designed to spare validators the work of repeatedly copying program data.

Anza’s November 20 tracker listed both switches as pending on Solana mainnet, with no activation slot for either.

The checks can reject a write to an account the program no longer owns, even while validators still use copied data.

Sources indicate that the paths show conditional runtime behavior. Their lengths carry no timing or performance measurement.

Conceptual diagram from SIMD-0460, the original runtime proposal and Agave’s implementation split. The same check branches to a rejected access or to two possible routes for an allowed access.

Recent findings suggest that the paths show conditional runtime behavior. Their lengths carry no timing or performance measurement.

The memory checks can reject a read that runs past the end of an account or a write to an account the program cannot modify. They also change the stack layout older programs use to hold temporary data. Code that relied on that layout can behave differently after the change. One documented failure involves how Solana programs hand accounts to one another within a transaction.

In a recent development, in the case described in an Anchor patch, one program calls another and transfers ownership of an account during the call. When the first program finishes, older Anchor code tries to write the account data back even when the bytes have stayed the same. The old runtime let that attempt pass. Under Solana’s newly introduced rules, the attempt fails because the first program has already given up the right to write to that account.

According to recent reports, the patch author notes programs that delegated accounts this way hit the error in production replay. A transaction that takes the affected path can fail while an app’s other transactions continue to go through.

Anza engineer Alexander Meißner wrote in the original runtime proposal that the team replayed mainnet traffic. The proposal says most developers whose apps would have failed in that exercise were contacted and had made fixes. Replay checks the instruction paths that appeared in the sample. A rarely used path can escape that check if the transactions Anza replayed never took it.

Meißner’s January 30 memory rules proposal states developers of the Agave and Firedancer validator clients split the original plan so earlier work could ship even if a later part needed more time. In Agave’s implementation discussion, Meißner described a separate testing problem. Combining the fresh rules and the copy change made it hard to tell intended changes in execution from mistakes. Giving the two changes separate switches let developers test the new rules with the old copying path still in place.

In the old execution path, the validator copies account data into a program’s virtual machine and takes it back when the program finishes. A call to another program adds another round trip. Meißner’s proposal describes up to four copies for an instruction with a single cross-program call. With direct mapping enabled, the virtual machine can access those account bytes where they already reside.

In a recent development, anza’s tracker lists the memory checks and the mapping switch one epoch apart on both testnet and devnet. On mainnet, the date to watch for affected apps is the activation of the memory checks. Validators get the copy savings when the mapping switch goes live.

Industry News: Tesla confirms rare upcoming delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its upcoming Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its upcoming Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

Sources indicate that but the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

Industry observers note that HMD took its first truck on November 2 and says it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler mentioned Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

The organization ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

In a recent development, owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

It has been revealed that tesla released volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

Industry observers note that so we’re left with proxies. Tesla says its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how substantial that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

The order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that demonstrates whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

It has been revealed that I think the semi is going to be a big seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

  • The latest FOMC minutes could be an early warning sign for Bitcoin’s Q4 outlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is Bitcoin’s worst Q4 on record getting closer?

In a recent development, the last 24 hours may have served as a reality check for investors. Bitcoin broke below the $62,000-level for the first time since August. However, the sharp decline may not be an isolated move. The sell-off followed the release of the latest FOMC minutes, adding to concerns over the Fed’s next policy move.

So, with Q4 already shaping up to be one of Bitcoin’s weakest quarters, could the worst be yet to come?

The latest FOMC minutes could be an early warning sign for Bitcoin’s Q4 outlook.

According to the minutes, almost all Fed officials now expect more rate hikes to bring inflation back to the 2% target. Some even suggested that a 50-basis-point hike could be on the table if inflation data worsens. In this context, Bitcoin’s latest correction suggests that investors may be taking a bearish view of the report. It is set to lay the tone for the next Fed meeting, scheduled for 10th December.

In short, the Fed maintained interest rates at 3.75%-4% in October, but the minutes have now strengthened expectations of another December hike. Here, it’s worth pointing out that market expectations already reflect this shift.

Sources indicate that according to CME data, for instance, the odds of a rate hike have reached 100%. Of this, 92.7% of traders expect a 25-basis-point hike, taking rates to 4%-4.25%. The remaining 7.3% expect a bigger, 50-basis-point hike to 4.25%-4.5%.

Meanwhile, the pressure is also showing up in traditional markets.

The Dollar Index rose to 103.82 on 18th November, its highest level since April 2025. As a result, yields on U.S 10-year Treasuries rose above 5.1%. Also, it seems increasingly likely that if this continues, traditional assets will become more appealing than riskier assets. This is likely due to the hawkish tone of the FOMC minutes which said,.

Almost all participants judged that further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate.

Bitcoin’s [BTC] Q4 decline is getting closer to its 2018 record now.

As the chart below highlights, Bitcoin is down 24.45% in Q4 2026, with November’s 18.48% decline accelerating the correction. This puts BTC on track for one of its weakest fourth quarters on record. The closest historical comparison is Q4 2018, when Bitcoin fell by 43.5% during the bear market.

Sure, the prevailing decline is still 19.05% short of that record. However, this is where the latest FOMC minutes come into play. The release has added to concerns across the crypto market, with traders now weighing the possibility of further rate hikes.

If these expectations continue to rise, Bitcoin could face more selling pressure, pushing its Q4 decline closer to the 2018 record.

However, the bigger question is whether this selling pressure can continue or not.

In a recent development, with rate hikes now almost fully priced in, the focus will shift to whether Bitcoin has enough demand to absorb further selling. This would make on-chain activity and institutional flows key indicators to watch. At the time of writing though, the signals were not encouraging.

In fact, according to a recent Wintermute report,.

With flows negative and the 200-week lost, December Fed hike is priced at about 92% after core CPI printed 0.3% for a third month, and spot Bitcoin ETFs are $1.9B net negative for 2026. We expect pressure into the $50s, with Saturday’s $62K low the first level and the $60K put cluster on Deribit the next magnet.

To understand how the macro environment could affect Bitcoin’s Q4 performance, the focus should also be on key on-chain data.

According to Glassnode’s latest report, Bitcoin has been facing strong selling pressure. Investors are booking losses at levels last seen near major market bottoms in 2018, 2020 and 2022. However, the $62K-66K range is acting as a key support zone, with nearly 20% of short-term holder supply sitting in this range.

It has been revealed that that’s not all though. According to CryptoQuant, Bitcoin’s 30-day Net Realized Profit/Loss dropped to -$8.4 billion recently, its lowest level since the summer. Selling has accelerated too, with investors realizing $5.4 billion in losses between 15th-18th November alone. Even long-term holders have been selling at a loss, with their SOPR falling to 0.73 — its lowest level since August.

The key takeaway? The ongoing losses are still lower than those seen during the February (30 billion) and June (18.4 billion) bottoms. This means that Bitcoin may not have reached full capitulation “yet.”.

So, if Bitcoin falls below $60K, this could lead to liquidations of nearly 20% of the short-term supply.

Considering the hawkish Fed, bearish technicals, and negative on-chain signals, a further downtrend cannot be ruled out. In fact, Wintermute now anticipates a further decline, with $50K now becoming a possible downside target for BTC.

The comparison with gold adds another layer to the picture.

In a recent development, from a technical perspective, Bitcoin has been flashing signs of some positive momentum relative to gold. On 18th November, the Bitcoin-to-Gold rate rose above its 200-day simple moving average to 17.13 ounces of gold for one Bitcoin. However, the broader trend might tell us a different story.

Despite this recovery, however, the BTC/XAU ratio was still down nearly 16% in Q4 at press time.

In other words, while Bitcoin has bounced against gold in the short term, it continues to underperform over the quarter. So, for long-term holders, gold still has the upper hand, while Bitcoin needs a stronger recovery to close the performance gap.

This finding also brings the cautious FOMC minutes back into focus.

Bitcoin now needs stronger spot demand, ETF inflows and a recovery in the BTC/XAU ratio to limit further losses. However, ongoing capitulation raises concerns about whether buyers can absorb the pressure. With the next FOMC meeting adding to market uncertainty, Wintermute’s $50K downside target will be in play.

Technically, that would pull Bitcoin nearly 40% lower in Q4. If selling pressure continues, the possibility of Bitcoin’s Q4 correction surpassing 2018’s record cannot be ruled out.

Bitcoin’s Q4 decline hit 24.45%, with weak on-chain data, ETF outflows, and hawkish Fed expectations adding to selling pressure.

A drop to $50K could push Bitcoin’s Q4 losses close to 40%, putting 2018’s record within reach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now notes Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.
  • On November 6, Musk mentioned Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now notes Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first announced it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a tech giant that sells cars to people.

On November 6, Musk mentioned Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

It has been revealed that the reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of strategy, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

It has been revealed that and the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

Sources indicate that some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

It has been revealed that the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

According to recent reports, that’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t revealed a single upcoming consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that launched in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Sources indicate that even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

According to recent reports, the pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car plans for Robotaxi in 2024. No latest consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

Recent findings suggest that A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

It has been revealed that tesla is becoming a company that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maple Finance’s disclosed Bitcoin addresses held 400 fewer BTC than the lender reported for its syrupUSDC stablecoin lending pool in a Nov. 18 snapshot, according to the blockchain data firm Bitquery. Bitquery counted 15,961 BTC at those addresses against the 16,361 BTC Maple reported through its public API. That accounted for 97.6% of the reported Bitcoin.

In its investigation, Bitquery estimated that the collateral it could account for across assets was worth about 152% of the roughly $847 million in syrupUSDC loans at that point. Bitquery reported that the disclosed holdings of Ether, wrapped Bitcoin and XRP matched Maple’s figures in the same check. Bitquery read loan balances from Maple’s smart contracts and checked the totals against the pools’ books. It calculated coverage against outstanding syrupUSDC loans alone.

In a recent development, depositors receive syrupUSDC when they supply USDC. Their yield comes from loans to institutional borrowers, who pledge crypto as collateral that can be sold to recover money if they stop paying.

Bitquery’s Nov. 18, 2026 snapshot measured Bitcoin balances at disclosed addresses and estimated the value of all collateral it could count against syrupUSDC loans.

Industry observers note that the 400 BTC gap concerns balances at disclosed addresses. The coverage estimate compares assets counted across the pool with its outstanding loans.

Industry observers note that balances and loan coverage reflect the Nov. 18 snapshot. The address difference does not identify who controlled the coins or establish whether the discrepancy persisted. The 152% estimate applies to the pool in aggregate.

The first bar splits Maple’s reported 16,361 BTC into 15,961 BTC at listed addresses and a 400 BTC difference. Dividing 15,961 by 16,361 and rounding to one decimal gives 97.6%. The second bar plots Bitquery’s approximate 152% coverage estimate with a 100% loan-balance marker.

Recent findings suggest that balances and loan coverage reflect the Nov. 18 snapshot. The address difference does not identify who controlled the coins or establish whether the discrepancy persisted. The 152% estimate applies to the pool in aggregate.

Recent findings suggest that bitquery took the reported amounts and wallet list from Maple’s public API on Nov. 18 and checked balances on Bitcoin, Ethereum and the XRP Ledger. Four of the 26 Bitcoin addresses it checked were empty. Bitquery stated coins from three had moved to an address outside the published list. The published amounts and addresses came from Maple. The blockchain data gave Bitquery a separate record of the balances at those addresses.

Bitquery published the investigation on Nov. 19 and stated balances could have changed between Maple’s upgrade and its read. The report leaves open how much of the difference those transfers explain and who controls the receiving wallet.

Sources indicate that maple Finance’s syrupUSDC dashboard demonstrated about 14,162 BTC on Nov. 21 and listed 35 collateral wallets across several assets. The later dashboard leaves the Nov. 18 gap unexplained and does not establish whether Maple added the receiving address.

Maple’s dashboard also links to a automated LedgerLens check by The Network Firm Tech & Services, which reported about $1.316 billion in syrupUSDC collateral at 01:00 UTC on Nov. 17. That check predates Bitquery’s snapshot. The provider indicates the service relies on Maple and third-party data, including custodians and on-chain records, and offers no audit opinion or assurance. The verification dashboard reports a dollar total for the pool at the time shown. It does not break that figure down by wallet.

According to recent reports, published addresses give depositors a way to check what the wallets held at a given time. Establishing who controls the coins and what Maple could sell if a borrower defaults requires evidence about custody and the loan terms.
